paper.title: Socioeconomic inequalities in survival to retirement age in Denmark: a register-based analysis
paper.code_data_availability: Data availability: 'Access to individual-level data is restricted by Danish law. …

registers.name_in_paper: Danish registries (Danish registry data, accessed through Statistics Denmark)
registers.role: sample frame, treatment (education, occupation, income), outcomes (deaths / survival), linkage

linkages: Individual-level records on all registered residents of Denmark, linked over 1986–2019 so that each person of the 1936–1954 cohorts is followed from age 45/50 to age 65 or 67
Family income linked at the household level: family members' individual disposable incomes summed and divided by the number of equivalent adults in the household

sample.universe: All individuals belonging to the 1936–1954 birth cohorts who were registered as resident in Denmark during the entire study period and were observed from age 45 onwards
sample.unit_of_observation: Individual followed from age 50 to age 65 or 67, aggregated into sex-, cohort- and SES-specific cohort partial life tables
selection_rules: Born in one of the 19 consecutive cohorts 1936–1954 ('complete cohorts', for which complete survival data are available)
Registered as resident in Denmark during the entire study period
Followed from the year they turn 50 until they reach either age 65 or age 67
Income data are missing for the 1936 cohort
Occupation data are only available for the 1942–1953 cohorts
For the 50–67 analyses, cohorts 1953 and 1954 are excluded because they did not reach age 67 within the study period

construction_notes: Categorical SES indicators: modal value observed between age 46 (or the earliest age available) and 50; continuous indicators: average value over the same window; both fixed for each individual over the whole study period
Education: highest attained level, three ISCED categories — low (primary and lower secondary), mid (upper secondary), high (tertiary)

Income: equivalized family disposable income (family members' individual disposable incomes summed, divided by the number of equivalent adults in the household), corrected for inflation, divided into quartiles by age, sex and cohort

Occupation: ISCO-based, three groups — lower manual (Skilled Agricultural, Forestry and Fishery Workers; Craft and Related Trades Workers); upper manual / lower non-manual (Plant and Machine Operators and Assemblers; Elementary Occupations; Technicians and Associate Professionals; Clerical Support Workers; Services and Sales Workers); upper non-manual (Managers and Professionals)
Sex-specific cohort partial life tables constructed between ages 50 and 67 for each sub-population; the probability of dying between ages 50 and 65 (and 50 and 67) is read off these tables

Average yearly rate of mortality improvement computed between the first (1936) and last (1954) cohort as r = −[ln(15q50^c2) − ln(15q50^c1)]/(c2 − c1), assuming a constant improvement from one cohort to the next
Ages of equivalent mortality computed against the highest-SES group's probability of dying between ages 50 and 65, assuming a proportional increase of the probability from one entire age to the next
Relative differences (ratios of probabilities) and partial lifespan variation reported in the Appendix

claims.statement: Across the 1936–1954 birth cohorts, the probability of dying between age 50 and 65 among all women changed at an average yearly rate of 2.38% (positive = improvement).

definition.value: Year of birth; the study follows 19 consecutive complete birth cohorts (1936–1954) from the year they turn 50 until they reach age 65 or 67, and compares the cohort-specific probability of dying across successive cohorts.

timing.value: Fixed at birth; cohorts observed from age 45/50 onwards over the register period 1986–2019.

outcome.label: Probability of dying between age 50 and 65 (15q50)

definition.value: Life-table probability of dying between exact age 50 and exact age 65, read off sex-specific cohort partial life tables constructed between ages 50 and 67 for each SES sub-population.

timing.value: Cumulated over the 15 years from age 50 to age 65, by birth cohort.

units.value: percent per successive birth cohort (average yearly rate of improvement in the probability of dying between ages 50 and 65; negative = worsening)

estimand.target_population: All women of the 1936–1954 Danish birth cohorts, registered as resident in Denmark over the whole study period
estimand.time_horizon: Probability of dying cumulated over the 15 years from age 50 to age 65; rate of change averaged over the 1936–1954 cohorts

population.description: All women, Danish registers 1986–2019
population.birth_cohorts: 1936–1954 (as stated in the Table 1 caption)
population.selection: All individuals of the 1936–1954 birth cohorts registered as resident in Denmark during the entire study period, observed from age 45 onwards

identification.source_of_variation: None: this is a descriptive cohort comparison. Differences across cohorts and SES groups are observed, not generated by a reform, lottery, discontinuity or instrument.

key_assumptions.assumption: Socioeconomic status measured between ages 46 and 50 and held fixed for the whole study period captures long-term SES rather than short-term fluctuations.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Stated as the motivation for fixing the computed values; for occupation the paper argues that modal occupation over the five years before age 50 avoids the incongruous shifts towards manual classes observed close to retirement age.

key_assumptions.assumption: Poor health before age 50 does not itself drive the measured SES (health-related reduction of income); the authors state they cannot completely exclude it.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Mitigation only: income is averaged over up to five years before age 50 rather than taken year by year; the paper concedes the bias cannot be completely excluded.

implies_edges.to: Probability of dying between age 50 and retirement age

key_assumptions.assumption: The analysis conditions on being registered as a resident of Denmark during the entire study period (a closed population: no in- or out-migration, observed from age 45 onwards).
key_assumptions.supported_by: Stated as an inclusion rule for the study population; no further evidence on how migrants differ is offered.

implies_edges.from: Registered as resident in Denmark during the entire study period

key_assumptions.assumption: Changes in the composition of SES groups across cohorts do not invalidate the across-cohort comparison of group-specific mortality.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Discussed as a limitation for education and occupation; the paper presents the compositional changes themselves (Fig. 1) and argues that income quartiles circumvent the problem by construction.

key_assumptions.assumption: Mortality improves at a constant rate from one cohort to the next, so that a single average yearly rate summarises the 1936–1954 change.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Stated when adapting the standard population-growth-rate equation; not tested.

threats_discussed: Compositional changes across cohorts in the educational and occupational groups being compared
Incongruous changes in occupational class towards manual workers close to retirement age, which could cause over-estimating the mortality of manual workers
Health-related reduction of income before age 50 (reverse causation / lagged selection), which the authors say they cannot completely exclude

Selection into higher socioeconomic groups on personal characteristics that are themselves associated with mortality (raised in the theoretical background, citing Dowd & Hamoudi, 2014; Fors et al., 2021)
robustness_checks: The same analyses repeated for mortality between ages 50 and 67 (Appendix Figure A1 and Table A1)
Relative rather than absolute differences: ratios of the probabilities of dying (Appendix, Figure A4)
Partial lifespan variation between ages 50 and 65 or 67 (Appendix Figure A2), which the paper says closely mirrors Fig. 2
Ages of equivalent mortality recomputed for mortality between ages 50 and 67 (Appendix Figure A3)
Three SES dimensions analysed separately; the paper states the results are robust to the selection of the SES indicator
unresolved_confounders: Health-related reduction of income before age 50 ('although we cannot completely exclude it')
Possible over-estimation of the mortality of manual workers caused by late-career changes in occupational class

estimator.value: Sex-specific cohort partial life tables (ages 50–67); average yearly rate of mortality improvement computed from the first (1936) and last (1954) cohort as r = −[ln(15q50^c2) − ln(15q50^c1)]/(c2 − c1). No regression is estimated.

estimation.specification: Unnumbered equation on p. 6 for the average yearly rate of mortality improvement, applied separately to each sex x SES sub-population

source_table.value: Table 1, p. 11, Female panel, row 'all women', column 'Rate'

heterogeneity.finding: Table 1: the average yearly rate of improvement is 2.38% for women and 1.58% for men; the text reports 2.4% versus 1.6%, against 1.9% for the total population.

timing.value: Fixed at birth; cohorts observed from age 45/50 onwards over the register period 1986–2019.

outcome.label: Probability of dying between age 50 and 65 (15q50)

definition.value: Life-table probability of dying between exact age 50 and exact age 65, read off sex-specific cohort partial life tables constructed between ages 50 and 67 for each SES sub-population.

timing.value: Cumulated over the 15 years from age 50 to age 65, by birth cohort.

units.value: percent per successive birth cohort (average yearly rate of improvement in the probability of dying between ages 50 and 65; negative = worsening)

identification.source_of_variation: None: this is a descriptive cohort comparison. Differences across cohorts and SES groups are observed, not generated by a reform, lottery, discontinuity or instrument.

key_assumptions.assumption: Socioeconomic status measured between ages 46 and 50 and held fixed for the whole study period captures long-term SES rather than short-term fluctuations.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Stated as the motivation for fixing the computed values; for occupation the paper argues that modal occupation over the five years before age 50 avoids the incongruous shifts towards manual classes observed close to retirement age.

key_assumptions.assumption: Poor health before age 50 does not itself drive the measured SES (health-related reduction of income); the authors state they cannot completely exclude it.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Mitigation only: income is averaged over up to five years before age 50 rather than taken year by year; the paper concedes the bias cannot be completely excluded.

implies_edges.to: Probability of dying between age 50 and retirement age

claims.statement: Across the 1936-1954 Danish birth cohorts, median average equivalized family disposable income at age 50 increased.

definition.value: Year of birth; the study follows 19 consecutive complete birth cohorts (1936–1954) from the year they turn 50 until they reach age 65 or 67, and compares the cohort-specific probability of dying across successive cohorts.

timing.value: Fixed at birth; cohorts observed from age 45/50 onwards over the register period 1986–2019.

outcome.label: Median average equivalized family disposable income at age 50

definition.value: Median of the average equivalized family disposable income computed over ages 46-50, by sex and birth cohort (the dots in Fig. 1 panel c).

timing.value: Measured at age 50 (categorical indicators: modal value over ages 46-50; continuous indicators: average over ages 46-50).

units.value: equivalized family disposable income (currency units; axis values not transcribed)

estimand.target_population: The Danish 1936-1954 birth cohorts observed at age 50
estimand.time_horizon: Measured at age 50, compared across the 1936-1954 birth cohorts

population.description: The Danish 1936-1954 birth cohorts at age 50
population.selection: All individuals of the 1936–1954 birth cohorts registered as resident in Denmark during the entire study period, observed from age 45 onwards

identification.source_of_variation: None: this is a descriptive cohort comparison. Differences across cohorts and SES groups are observed, not generated by a reform, lottery, discontinuity or instrument.

key_assumptions.assumption: Socioeconomic status measured between ages 46 and 50 and held fixed for the whole study period captures long-term SES rather than short-term fluctuations.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Stated as the motivation for fixing the computed values; for occupation the paper argues that modal occupation over the five years before age 50 avoids the incongruous shifts towards manual classes observed close to retirement age.

key_assumptions.assumption: The analysis conditions on being registered as a resident of Denmark during the entire study period (a closed population: no in- or out-migration, observed from age 45 onwards).
key_assumptions.supported_by: Stated as an inclusion rule for the study population; no further evidence on how migrants differ is offered.

implies_edges.from: Registered as resident in Denmark during the entire study period

threats_discussed: Compositional changes across cohorts in the educational and occupational groups being compared
Incongruous changes in occupational class towards manual workers close to retirement age, which could cause over-estimating the mortality of manual workers
Health-related reduction of income before age 50 (reverse causation / lagged selection), which the authors say they cannot completely exclude

Selection into higher socioeconomic groups on personal characteristics that are themselves associated with mortality (raised in the theoretical background, citing Dowd & Hamoudi, 2014; Fors et al., 2021)
robustness_checks: The same analyses repeated for mortality between ages 50 and 67 (Appendix Figure A1 and Table A1)
Relative rather than absolute differences: ratios of the probabilities of dying (Appendix, Figure A4)
Partial lifespan variation between ages 50 and 65 or 67 (Appendix Figure A2), which the paper says closely mirrors Fig. 2
Ages of equivalent mortality recomputed for mortality between ages 50 and 67 (Appendix Figure A3)
Three SES dimensions analysed separately; the paper states the results are robust to the selection of the SES indicator
unresolved_confounders: Health-related reduction of income before age 50 ('although we cannot completely exclude it')
Possible over-estimation of the mortality of manual workers caused by late-career changes in occupational class

estimator.value: Cell shares (panels a and b) and quartiles of the income distribution (panel c) computed by sex and birth cohort on the register population. No model is estimated.

source_table.value: Figure 1, panel c, p. 7; described in the text on p. 6

heterogeneity.finding: Distributions differ for men and women: women from later cohorts were more present in the low and high education categories, the female occupational composition shifted away from lower manual work while the male composition changed little, and women had slightly higher median incomes than men in the youngest cohorts.
